definition: M-type bright giants are [bright giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bright_giant) ([luminosity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_class) II) [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M.
[[Stellar classification#Class M|Spectral type-M]] brown dwarfs are the hottest, and therefore youngest, [brown dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_dwarf)s.

M-type giants are [giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_star) ([luminosity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_class) III) [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M.

M-type main-sequence stars are [main-sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence) [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s (usually [luminosity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_class) V) of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M.

M-type pre-main-sequence stars are stars of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M that have not yet reached their [main sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence) stage of evolution.

M-type subdwarfs are [subdwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdwarf) (typically [luminosity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_class) VI or prefix sd) [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M.

M-type supergiants are [supergiant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergiant) ([luminosity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminosity_class) I) [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s of [spectral type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_type) M.

Main-sequence stars, also called dwarf stars, are [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s that [fuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion) [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen) in their cores.

definition: Cosmic ray astronomy is a branch of [observational astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_astronomy) where scientists attempt to identify and study the potential sources of extremely high-energy (ranging from 1 [MeV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MeV) to more than 1 [EeV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EeV)) charged particles called [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays) coming from [outer space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space).

definition: Cosmic strings are hypothetical 1-dimensional [topological defect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_defect)s which may have formed during a [symmetry-breaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_breaking) [phase transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_phase_transition) in the early universe when the [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) of the [vacuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_state) manifold associated to this symmetry breaking was not [simply connected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simply_connected_space).

Cosmic time, or cosmological time, is the [time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time) [coordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate) used in the [Big Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang) models of [physical cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_cosmology).

The Cosmic Tradition is a series of six volumes, and also a [cosmological doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_Philosophy), authored by [Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Théon) and [Alma Théon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_Théon) around the turn of the 20th century.

Cosmic wind is a powerful [cosmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmos) stream of [charged particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charged_particle)s that can push [interstellar dust clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_cloud) of low density into [intergalactic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergalactic_space).

Cosmic-Ray Extremely Distributed Observatory (CREDO) is a scientific project initiated at the end of August 2016 by Polish scientists from the [Institute of Nuclear Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Nuclear_Physics_Polish_Academy_of_Sciences) in [Kraków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraków) (researchers from the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary also joined the project) whose purpose is the detection of [cosmic ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray)s and the search for [dark matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter).
cosmic-ray observatory is a scientific installation built to detect high-energy-particles coming from space called [cosmic ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray)s.

Cosmochemistry () or chemical cosmology is the study of the chemical composition of matter in the [universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe) and the processes that led to those compositions.

Cosmogenic nuclides (or cosmogenic isotopes) are rare [nuclide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclide)s ([isotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope)s) created when a high-energy [cosmic ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray) interacts with the [nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus) of an [in situ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_situ) Solar System [atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom), causing nucleons (protons and neutrons) to be expelled from the atom (see [cosmic ray spallation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray_spallation)).

cosmological constant problem or vacuum catastrophe is the substantial disagreement between the observed values of [vacuum energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_energy) [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_density) (the small value of the [cosmological constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_constant)) and the much larger theoretical value of [zero-point energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-point_energy) suggested by [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory).

cosmological horizon is one of two boundaries in three dimensional space, the [particle horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_horizon) or the [event horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_horizon).

Cosmological natural selection, also called the fecund universes, is a hypothesis proposed by [Lee Smolin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Smolin) intended as a scientific alternative to the [anthropic principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic_principle).
cosmological phase transition is an overall change in the [state of matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_matter) across the whole universe.

cosmological principle is the notion that the spatial distribution of matter in the universe is uniformly [isotropic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotropy) and [homogeneous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneity_(physics)) when viewed on a large enough scale, since the forces are expected to act equally throughout the universe on a large scale, and should, therefore, produce no observable inequalities in the large-scale structuring over the course of evolution of the matter field that was initially laid down by the [Big Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang).

dark flow is a controversial hypothesis to explain certain non-random measurements of [peculiar velocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peculiar_velocity) of [galaxy cluster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_cluster)s.

dark forest hypothesis is the idea that [extraterrestrial civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterrestrial_life) may exist in abundance across the universe, but remain silent and hidden out of fear that revealing themselves would lead to destruction by a more technologically advanced and hostile civilization.

dark galaxy is a hypothesized [galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy) with [dark matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter) but no, or very few, [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star).
Dark globular cluster is a proposed type of [globular star clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globular_star_clusters) that has an unusually high mass for the number of stars within it.

definition: dark photon (also hidden, heavy, para-, or secluded photon) is a hypothetical [hidden sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_sector) [particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_particle), proposed as a [force carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_carrier) similar to the [photon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photon) of [electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetism) but potentially connected to [dark matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter).

dark star is a theoretical object compatible with [Newtonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonian_mechanics) that, due to its large mass, has a surface [escape velocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_velocity) that equals or exceeds the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light).

definition: Gravitational collapse is the contraction of an [astronomical object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_object) due to the influence of its own [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity), which tends to draw matter inward toward the [center of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_gravity).

gravitational compression is a phenomenon in which [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity), acting on the [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass) of an object, compresses it, reducing its size and increasing the object's [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density).

gravitational lens is matter, such as a [cluster of galaxies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_cluster) or a [point particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_particle), that bends [light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light) from a distant source as it travels toward an observer.

definition: Gravitational memory effects, also known as gravitational-wave memory effects, are predicted persistent changes in the relative position of pairs of masses in space due to the passing of a [gravitational wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave) (GW).

Gravitational scattering is the alteration of trajectories when two or more [celestial objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_objects) exchange [energy and momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_energy) through close [gravitational encounters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_fields).

gravitational self-force formalism is an approach to solving the [relativistic two body problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_two_body_problem) using a systematic expansion of the dynamics is powers of the ratio of the masses of the two components of the binary.

gravitational singularity, spacetime singularity, or simply singularity, is a theoretical condition in which [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_field) is predicted to be so intense that [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime) itself would break down catastrophically.

Gravitational waves are [waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave) of [spacetime curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curved_spacetime) that propagate at the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light) and are produced by the relative [motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion) of [gravitating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity) [masses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass).

definition: gravitational wave background (also GWB and stochastic background) is a random background of [gravitational wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave)s permeating the [Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe), which is detectable by gravitational-wave experiments, like [pulsar timing array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulsar_timing_array)s.

Gravitational-wave astronomy is a subfield of [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy) concerned with the detection and study of [gravitational wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_wave)s emitted by astrophysical sources.

gravitational-wave detector (used in a gravitational-wave observatory) is any device designed to measure tiny distortions of [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime) called [gravitational waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_waves).

intergalactic star, also known as an intracluster star or a rogue star, is a [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star) not [gravitationally bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitationally_bound) to any [galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy).

Intermediate Luminosity Optical Transient (ILOT) is an astronomical object which undergoes an optically detectable explosive event with an [absolute magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_magnitude) (M) brighter than a [classical nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_nova) (M ~ −8) but fainter than that of a supernova (M ~ −17).

Intermediate Luminosity Red Transients (ILRT), is a subclass of stellar transients that occupy the luminosity gap between [classical nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_nova) and typical [supernovae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernovae).

intermediate spiral galaxy is a [galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy) that is in between the classifications of a [barred spiral galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barred_spiral_galaxy) and an [unbarred spiral galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbarred_spiral_galaxy).

Internal heat is the [heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat) source from the interior of [celestial object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_object)s, such as [star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star)s, [brown dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_dwarf)s, [planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet)s, [moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_satellite), [dwarf planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwarf_planet)s, and (in the early history of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System)) even [asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid)s such as [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta), resulting from contraction caused by [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitation) (the [Kelvin–Helmholtz mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin–Helmholtz_mechanism)), [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion), [tidal heating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_heating), core solidification ([heat of fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_of_fusion) released as molten core material solidifies), and [radioactive decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay).

definition: Newton Lacy Pierce Prize in Astronomy is awarded annually by the [American Astronomical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Astronomical_Society) to a young (less than age 36) [astronomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomer) for outstanding achievement in observational astronomical research.

Newton's law of universal gravitation describes [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity) as a [force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force) by stating that every [particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle) attracts every other particle in the universe with a force that is [[Proportionality (mathematics)#Direct proportionality|proportional]] to their masses and [[Proportionality (mathematics)#Inverse proportionality|inversely proportional]] to the square of the distance between their centers of mass.
Newtonian gauge is a perturbed form of the [Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker line element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLRW_metric).
